# Ageism and Employment

This section takes the Fraboni Scale on Ageism and attempts to make it more
applicable to an employment scenario. The questions are divided into two
sections. First, we ask people about their own views of older co-workers to
assess a level of ageism, and then we ask about their feelings towards 
continuing education - both in terms of their own skilling up, as well as their
views of older co-workers value with continuing education.

I will run a Spearman's analysis on the two averages to determine if there is
any correlation between the two to help answer Research Question 2.

```{r}
#| label: set-ae-Setup
#| echo: false
#| include: false

library('tidyverse')
library('ggthemes')

source("_recode_likert.R")

source("_graph_standards_bar.R")

main_df <- readRDS("main_df.rds")
```

## Questions Scale

All questions in this section use a 5 Point Likert Scale with the following 
point values:

- 1 = Strongly Disagree
- 2 = Somewhat Disagree
- 3 = Neither Agree nor Disagree
- 4 = Somewhat Agree
- 5 = Strongly Agree

## Vector Definitions

```{r}
#| label: vdf-ae-VectorDefinitions

# Map to convert Ageism_Employment Likert scale answers to numbers. Includes 
# both normal and reverse mappings.

ageism_employment_map <- list(
  normal = c(
    "Strongly Disagree"          = 1, 
    "Somewhat Disagree"          = 2,
    "Neither Agree nor Disagree" = 3,
    "Somewhat Agree"             = 4, 
    "Strongly Agree"             = 5
  ),
  reverse = c(
    "Strongly Agree"             = 1,
    "Somewhat Agree"             = 2, 
    "Neither Agree nor Disagree" = 3,
    "Somewhat Disagree"          = 4,
    "Strongly Disagree"          = 5
  )
)


# Like the original Fraboni Scale of Ageism, I wanted to create reverse  
# scaled questions to help add validity to the the questions. This is a 
# character vector of those reverse scaled questions.

reverse_scale_variables <- c("Ageism_Employment_2",
                             "Ageism_Employment_5",
                             "Ageism_Employment_19")


# This is a character vector with the questions associated with Continuing 
# Education questions.

ce_variables <- c("Ageism_Employment_12",
                  "Ageism_Employment_13",
                  "Ageism_Employment_14",
                  "Ageism_Employment_15",
                  "Ageism_Employment_16",
                  "Ageism_Employment_17",
                  "Ageism_Employment_18",
                  "Ageism_Employment_19")

# Short Label Vectors with Question Wording for graphing purposes. Ageist
# are the ageist questions and ce are the Continuing Education questions. The
# [R] indicates Reverse Scaled.

short_labels_ageist <- c(
  "Ageism_Employment_1"  = "Q1: Forced retirement after a certain age",
  "Ageism_Employment_2"  = "Q2: Prefer same-age coworkers [R]",
  "Ageism_Employment_3"  = "Q3: Skills no longer applicable",
  "Ageism_Employment_4"  = "Q4: Don't understand today's tech",
  "Ageism_Employment_5"  = "Q5: Enjoy diverse age groups [R]",
  "Ageism_Employment_6"  = "Q6: Less to offer than younger workers",
  "Ageism_Employment_7"  = "Q7: Harder to work with",
  "Ageism_Employment_8"  = "Q8: Prefer same-age socializing",
  "Ageism_Employment_9"  = "Q9: Older workers didn't save enough",
  "Ageism_Employment_10" = "Q10: Less technologically savvy",
  "Ageism_Employment_11" = "Q11: Don't stay current with trends"
)

short_labels_ce <- c(
  "Ageism_Employment_12" = "Q12: Important to earn certifications",
  "Ageism_Employment_13" = "Q13: Older workers w/ CE easier to work with",
  "Ageism_Employment_14" = "Q14: Staying current is critical to success",
  "Ageism_Employment_15" = "Q15: Not staying current is biggest issue",
  "Ageism_Employment_16" = "Q16: CE makes older workers more competent",
  "Ageism_Employment_17" = "Q17: Higher respect for those who pursue CE",
  "Ageism_Employment_18" = "Q18: CE important for IT career success",
  "Ageism_Employment_19" = "Q19: Don't need CE to stay competent [R]"
)
```

## Create a data frame specific to Ageism & Employment

Create an Ageism Employment DataFrame with ID and answers to the Ageism 
Employment questions.

```{r}
#| label: cde-ae-CreateDataFrame

ageism_employment_df <- main_df |>
  select(ID, starts_with("Ageism_Employment_"))
```

## Recode the DataFrame

Re-code the data frame with the associated numbers including those that need to 
be reverse scored.

```{r}
#| label: cde-ae-RecodeDataFrame

ageism_employment_df <- recode_likert(ageism_employment_df,
                                      "Ageism_Employment_",
                                      ageism_employment_map$normal,
                                      ageism_employment_map$reverse,
                                      reverse_scale_variables)
```

## Cleaning up NA Values.

Investigate the number of NA Values across the data frame.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ae-NACounts
#| tbl-cap: Number of Missing Values from Ageism & Employment Section

ageism_employment_df |> 
  mutate(na_count = rowSums(is.na(across(everything())))) |>
  filter(na_count > 0) |>
  select(ID, na_count) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("ID", "Num Missing"))
               
```

This section has 19 questions and the dataframe has 20 variables. Since the ID 
represents one of those variables, I am just going to drop every row that has 
more than 18 NAs since these are clearly unusable in this analysis. Here I build 
the dataframe with only the results that have less than or equal to 18 responses 
and verify the results.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ae-NewNACounts
#| tbl-cap: Missing Values after Dropping Significant Entries

ageism_employment_df <- ageism_employment_df |>
  filter(rowSums(is.na(across(everything()))) <= 18)

ageism_employment_df |> 
  mutate(na_count = rowSums(is.na(across(everything())))) |>
  filter(na_count > 0) |>
  select(ID, na_count) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("ID", "Num Missing"))
```

## Further cleanup

The most NAs is 2 with only 7 rows having them at all. Since this section had a 
neutral answer of '3', we can simply replace these with that value.

```{r}
#| label: cde-ae-FillNeutrals

ageism_employment_df <- ageism_employment_df |>
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ replace(., is.na(.), 3)))
```

## Post Dataframe Manipulation Information:

Any NAs in data frame: ***`r anyNA(ageism_employment_df)`***

Number of Research Participants for Ageism & Employment Analysis is: 
***`r nrow(ageism_employment_df)`***

## Save Out Ageism Employment Data Frame
We will be using this cleaned data frame in our Correlation Analysis.

```{r}
#| label: cde-ae-SaveDataFrame

saveRDS(ageism_employment_df, 
        "ageism_employment_df.rds")
```

## Feelings toward Continuing Education

To answer one of my research questions, I need to address participants feelings 
toward continuing education. These are questions 12 - 19.

```{r}
#| label: cde-ae-CESetup

ce_df <- ageism_employment_df |>
  select(ID, all_of(ce_variables))

summary(ce_df)
```

## Response Distributions

### General Ageist Beliefs (Q1–11)

These questions measure general ageist attitudes toward older workers in the IT
workplace. All items are scored 1–5 where higher scores indicate stronger 
agreement with the statement. Reverse-scored items (Q2, Q5) have been recoded so 
that higher scores remain consistent in direction with the rest of the scale.

```{r}
#| label: cde-ae-BuildDataFrames

# Calculate the Ageism & Employment averages on the entire question set.
ae_means <- ageism_employment_df |>
  select(-ID) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), ~as.numeric(as.character(.)))) |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~mean(., na.rm = TRUE))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "question", values_to = "mean") |>
  mutate(mean_label = as.character(round(mean, 2)))

# Calculate the averages for just the first set of questions.
# Regular Ageist Type Questions
ageist_means <- ae_means |>
  filter(question %in% names(short_labels_ageist)) |>
  mutate(
    label = short_labels_ageist[question],
    # Order levels lowest-to-highest so highest appears at top of horizontal 
    # chart
    label = factor(label, levels = label[order(mean)])
  )

# Calculate the averages for just the last set of questions
# Continuing Education Based
ce_means <- ae_means |>
  filter(question %in% names(short_labels_ce)) |>
  mutate(
    label = short_labels_ce[question],
    label = factor(label, levels = label[order(mean)])
  )
```

There is a strong feeling towards a preference of working with like-aged 
coworkers. Not nearly as strong, but still significant is the preference of
socializing with like-aged co-workers. The rest of the questions ordered by 
their strength don't show strong ageist views.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ae-AgeistBarChart
#| fig-cap: |
#|  General Ageist Beliefs Toward Older IT Workers<br>
#|  Mean response per question (1 = Strongly Disagree 5 = Strongly Agree)
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-height: 8
#| warning: false

graph_bar_chart(
  df          = ageist_means,
  x_category  = "label",
  y_category  = "mean",
  label_col   = "mean_label",
  x_label     = "Survey Question",
  y_label     = "Mean Score (1–5)",
  horizontal  = TRUE
)
```

Graphing the same data using a Violin Chart gives us a better idea how responses
varied to the questions.

Kernel Density Estimate is used here and causes some values outside the scale 
range not to be displayed. This does not impact the data being displayed.

The wider the graph, the more the responses cluster together. The Box Plot
inside the clusters indicates the Interquartile Range (IQR) with the darker
vertical line indicating the median.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ae-AgeistViolinChart
#| fig-cap: |
#|  General Ageist Beliefs Toward Older IT Workers<br>
#|  Response distribution per question 
#|  (1 = Strongly Disagree 5 = Strongly Agree)
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-height: 8
#| warning: false

ageism_employment_df |>
  select(-ID) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), ~as.numeric(as.character(.)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "question", values_to = "score") |>
  filter(question %in% names(short_labels_ageist)) |>
  mutate(
    label = short_labels_ageist[question],
    label = factor(label, levels = names(sort(tapply(score, label, median))))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = label, y = score)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "#4472C4", alpha = 0.6, trim = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, fill = "white", outlier.shape = NA) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:5, limits = c(0.5, 5.5)) +
  labs(
    x = "Survey Question",
    y = "Score (1–5)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Continuing Education Attitudes (Q12–19)

These questions measure attitudes toward continuing education and its 
relationship to perceptions of older IT workers. Higher scores indicate stronger 
agreement that CE is valuable and that older workers who pursue it are viewed 
more favorably.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ae-ContinuingEducationAttitudes
#| fig-cap: |
#|  Attitudes Toward Continuing Education<br>
#|  Mean response per question (1 = Strongly Disagree
#|  "5 = Strongly Agree
#| fig-height: 8
#| out-width: "100%"

graph_bar_chart(
  df          = ce_means,
  x_category  = "label",
  y_category  = "mean",
  label_col   = "mean_label",
  x_label     = "Survey Question",
  y_label     = "Mean Score (1–5)",
  horizontal  = TRUE
)
```

## Research Question 2 Analysis

To directly address Research Question 2, a composite score is computed for each
respondent in both question areas:

* General Ageist Beliefs (Q1–11)
* Continuing Education Attitudes  (Q12-19)

A Spearman rank correlation is run between them. A negative correlation would 
support the hypothesis that valuing Continuing Education is associated with 
holding fewer ageist beliefs toward older IT workers.

Spearman's ρ is used because both composites are means of ordinal Likert 
responses. No normality assumption is required.

## Composite Scores

```{r AE RQ2 Composite}
composites <- ageism_employment_df |>
  mutate(across(-ID, ~as.numeric(as.character(.)))) |>
  mutate(
    ageist_composite = rowMeans(across(
      Ageism_Employment_1:Ageism_Employment_11),
                                na.rm = TRUE),
    ce_composite     = rowMeans(
      across(Ageism_Employment_12:Ageism_Employment_19),
                                na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  select(ID, ageist_composite, ce_composite)

composites |>
  summarise(
    across(c(ageist_composite, ce_composite),
           list(N    = ~sum(!is.na(.)),
                Mean = ~round(mean(., na.rm = TRUE), 2),
                SD   = ~round(sd(.,   na.rm = TRUE), 2),
                Min  = ~round(min(., na.rm = TRUE),  2),
                Max  = ~round(max(., na.rm = TRUE),  2)))
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(),
               names_to  = c("Scale", "Stat"),
               names_sep = "_(?=[^_]+$)") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Stat, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(Scale = case_when(
    Scale == "ageist_composite" ~ "Ageist Beliefs (Q1–11)",
    Scale == "ce_composite"     ~ "CE Attitudes (Q12–19)",
    TRUE                        ~ Scale
  )) |>
  knitr::kable(align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

The ageist beliefs composite 
(mean = `r round(mean(composites$ageist_composite), 2)`, 
SD = `r round(sd(composites$ageist_composite), 2)`) sits well below the scale 
midpoint of 3.0, confirming the sample generally does not hold strong ageist 
beliefs. The CE composite (mean = `r round(mean(composites$ce_composite), 2)`, 
SD = `r round(sd(composites$ce_composite), 2)`) sits above the midpoint, 
reflecting broad agreement that continuing education is important for ones 
career.

## Spearman Correlation

I perform the Spearman Correlation against the composite scores of the two 
question sections.

```{r AE RQ2 Spearman}
cor_result <- cor.test(composites$ageist_composite,
                       composites$ce_composite,
                       method = "spearman",
                       exact  = FALSE)
cor_result
```

## Research Question 2 Interpretation

The Spearman correlation between CE attitudes and ageist beliefs is 
ρ = `r round(cor_result$estimate, 3)` (p = `r round(cor_result$p.value, 3)`). 
This is not statistically significant at α being 0.05, and the effect size is 
negligible.

## Conclusion

Generally people value continuing education in IT.

Generally, people do not have strong ageist views towards their older 
co-workers.

For Research Question 2 **We fail to reject the null hypothesis.** The data does 
not support a significant relationship between how strongly a respondent values 
continuing education and how ageist their general beliefs about older IT workers 
are.

This is a noteworthy finding. While individual continuing education questions 
(Q13, Q16) show that respondents believe older workers who pursue continuing 
education are viewed more favorably, this aggregate analysis suggests that 
holding positive continuing education attitudes does not translate into 
measurably lower ageist beliefs at the individual level. The relationship 
between continuing education and ageism in the IT workforce may be more nuanced 
than a direct correlation captures, and warrants further investigation.
